title: Strict Low-High Zigzag
statement:
Rearrange the array nums in place so that it zigzags strictly: nums[0] < nums[1] > nums[2] < nums[3] > …. Every odd index must hold a value strictly larger than both its neighbours.

The input is guaranteed to allow such an arrangement. Many arrangements may work; any valid one is accepted. The function returns nothing; the checker reads your array.

examples.why: Placing the sorted values small-big-small-big from the left gives 4 5 5 6, where 5 > 5 fails. Taking each half from its large end keeps the two 5s apart.
Two values: the smaller one goes first.

hints: Sort a copy. The even slots should get the smaller half and the odd slots the larger half. Which order inside each half avoids equal neighbours?
If the middle value repeats, it can end up in both halves. Place both halves from their large end, so those copies land far apart: one near the left, one near the right.
Even slots 0, 2, 4, … take the small half from largest to smallest; odd slots 1, 3, 5, … take the large half from largest to smallest. With values capped at 5000, counting sort makes it O(n).

explain.intuition:
Split the sorted values into a small half (the even slots, there are ⌈n/2⌉ of them) and a large half (the odd slots). Any small value is at most any large value, so the zigzag can only fail where the two halves share a value, which can only be the median.

Copies of the median sit at the top of the small half and the bottom of the large half. If both halves are written from their largest value first, the small half's median copies land at the left end of the even slots and the large half's copies land at the right end of the odd slots. They never become neighbours, as long as an answer exists at all. Writing both halves smallest first does the opposite and puts them side by side, as the first example shows.
steps: Sort a copy s of nums. Let m = ⌈n / 2⌉, the number of even slots.
Fill even slots 0, 2, 4, … with s[m−1], s[m−2], …, s[0].
Fill odd slots 1, 3, 5, … with s[n−1], s[n−2], …, s[m].
For O(n): count each value (they are at most 5000) and hand out values from the largest down, first to the odd slots, then to the even slots.
pitfalls: Interleaving the halves smallest first. [4, 5, 5, 6] becomes 4 5 5 6 with two equal neighbours.
Sorting and swapping neighbours (1,2), (3,4), …. That gives a non-strict wiggle (≤ ≥), not a strict one.
Writing into nums while still reading from it. Read from a sorted copy or from the counts.

complexity.time: O(n log n), or O(n + V) with counting

solutions.title: Sort and interleave halves in reverse
solutions.idea: Sorted copy; even slots get the small half from its top down, odd slots the large half from its top down.

solutions.title: Counting sort, largest values first
solutions.idea: Values are at most 5000. Hand out values from the largest down: first to odd slots, then to even slots.

followups: Do it in O(n) time and O(1) extra space: find the median with quickselect, then three-way partition through a remapped index.
Relax the rule to nums[0] ≤ nums[1] ≥ nums[2] ≤ …. Why does a single pass of neighbour swaps now suffice?
